I tell my attendants,Right there, When they rub me where it itches. They rub for a few seconds, then move on, There’s so much of it to wash, “It” being me, a former person, Now something that must be washed every day In so little time. Fifty minutes outside my breathing machine, And all I can do is stare As my breath recedes like the woman Who would not love me. It’s almost over, I say over and over to myself As soon as the machine is turned off. An idiotic mantra perhaps, But it helps when the ache descends into my eyes And my words quit coming out right.Left hand, I say.Right foot? the attendant says, guessing. I begin to fantasize about gusts of air Rushing down my windpipe with hurricane force. Garish and impossible, they’re respiratory porn. My re-entry is stalled By the attendant straightening a sheet That no one will see. Enraged, I squeeze my eyes closed.Christ. “What?”Never mind. Once back in and turned on, I cough violently and with conviction. Shocked by the force of the inrushing air, I feel my lungs expand like birthday balloons, My terror-flattened mind pops up into 3-D, As I return to the land of breathing. January, 1990

prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Right, When, They

outputs.L1:
I tell my attendants, “Right there,”  
when they rub the place where it itches.  
They rub for a few seconds, then move on.  
There is so much of it to wash—  
“it” being me, a former person,  
now something that must be washed every day  
in so little time.

Fifty minutes outside my breathing machine,  
and all I can do is stare  
as my breath recedes like the woman  
who would not love me.

“It’s almost over,” I say, over and over to myself  
as soon as the machine is turned off.  
An idiotic mantra, perhaps,  
but it helps when the ache descends into my eyes  
and my words stop coming out right.

“Left hand,” I say.

“Right foot?” the attendant says, guessing.

I begin to fantasize about gusts of air  
rushing down my windpipe with hurricane force.  
Garish and impossible, they are respiratory porn.

My re-entry is stalled  
by the attendant straightening a sheet  
that no one will see.  
Enraged, I squeeze my eyes closed.

“Christ.”

“What?”

“Never mind.”

Once back in and turned on,  
I cough violently and with conviction.  
Shocked by the force of the inrushing air,  
I feel my lungs expand like birthday balloons.  
My terror-flattened mind rises into 3-D  
as I return to the land of breathing.

January 1990
outputs.L2:
I direct my caregivers:  
“Here. That spot.”  
when their hands find the place that itches.  
They scratch briefly,  
then continue elsewhere.  

There is so much to clean—  
“it” meaning my body,  
what used to be a person,  
and is now a thing  
that has to be bathed daily  
within a painfully short span.  

I have fifty minutes away from my ventilator,  
and I can only look on  
while my breathing slips farther from me,  
like the woman  
who refused to love me.  

“It will be done soon,”  
I repeat silently  
the moment the machine is switched off.  
Maybe it is a foolish little chant,  
but it steadies me  
when pain settles behind my eyes  
and my speech starts failing.  

“Left hand,” I say.  

“Right foot?” the attendant asks,  
trying to interpret me.  

I start imagining torrents of air  
blasting through my trachea  
with the violence of a hurricane.  
The images are lurid, absurd—  
a kind of breathing fantasy.  

My return to the machine is delayed  
because the attendant is smoothing a sheet  
that nobody will notice.  
Furious,  
I clamp my eyes shut.  

“Christ.”  

“What?”  

“Forget it.”  

Once I am reconnected  
and the ventilator is running again,  
I cough hard,  
with full intensity.  
Startled by the power  
of the air flooding back in,  
I feel my lungs swell  
like balloons at a birthday party.  
My fear-crushed mind  
springs back into dimension,  
and I cross back  
into the world of breathing.  

January, 1990
outputs.L3:
The speaker is completely dependent on attendants to wash and care for their body during the short interval when they are disconnected from the breathing machine. This time is limited and tense, because every moment away from the machine brings the speaker closer to physical distress. What might otherwise be a routine act of care becomes an urgent and frightening experience, shaped by the speaker’s reliance on others and by the strict limits of their body.

As the machine is turned off, the speaker feels their breath begin to fade. Fear rises quickly as the body struggles without the mechanical support it needs to survive. The loss of air is not simply uncomfortable; it is terrifying. The speaker becomes intensely aware of each passing second, of the weakening breath, and of the possibility that the attendants may not understand how desperate the situation feels.

This fear is made worse by the difficulty of communication. The speaker cannot easily explain what they need or how much distress they are experiencing. Attempts to communicate with the attendant lead to frustration, because the speaker feels unheard or misunderstood. Their dependence on someone else becomes emotionally painful as well as physically dangerous, since they must trust another person to interpret their needs correctly and act quickly.

While waiting to be reconnected, the speaker begins to fantasize about air returning with force and abundance. They imagine powerful air rushing into their lungs, filling the empty space and restoring what has been lost. This fantasy shows how intensely the speaker longs for breath and how completely air has become associated with safety, freedom, and life itself.

When the breathing machine is finally reattached, relief arrives violently. Air enters the speaker’s body again, bringing not calm comfort but an overwhelming return to life. The reconnection restores the speaker’s sense of existence, as though the machine gives back not only breath but also identity, strength, and survival. The experience reveals both the fragility of the speaker’s body and the profound dependence on technology and caregivers that makes continued life possible.
outputs.L4:
The poem presents the experience of a ventilator-dependent speaker who is briefly taken off the breathing machine while attendants wash their body. What should be an ordinary act of care becomes terrifying, humiliating, and physically overwhelming. Without the ventilator, the speaker is forced into an acute awareness of the body’s vulnerability: breath is no longer automatic, privacy disappears, and the self is reduced to exposed flesh handled by others. The washing scene is described in stark bodily detail, emphasizing the indignity of being dependent on strangers for even the most intimate forms of care.

At the same time, the poem uses darkly comic metaphor to capture the absurdity of the situation. The speaker’s wit does not erase the fear, but it allows them to retain some control over how the experience is understood. Humor becomes a form of resistance against helplessness, a way of insisting that the speaker remains observant, intelligent, and fully human even when physically powerless.

When the ventilator is restored and air begins to flow again, the moment feels like a return to life itself. Breathing is not presented as a simple bodily function but as the condition that makes thought, speech, identity, and dignity possible. The poem therefore reveals how fragile personhood can become under extreme physical dependence. It shows that communication and selfhood are not abstract qualities; they are tied to breath, care, bodily autonomy, and the recognition of one’s humanity by others.
outputs.L5:
**Right, When, They**

Doing what is **right** is not always easy. Sometimes people know the correct choice, but they hesitate because the situation is difficult. **When** challenges appear, true character is often revealed. It is in those moments that people must decide whether to follow what is fair, honest, and kind.

**They** may face pressure from others, fear of failure, or uncertainty about the future. Still, choosing the right path can bring peace and confidence. Even small actions—helping someone, telling the truth, or standing up for fairness—can make a meaningful difference.

In the end, doing what is right matters most when it is hardest to do. When people choose wisely, they help create a better world for everyone.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a free-verse poem in the voice of a severely disabled person briefly disconnected from a breathing machine while attendants wash them, capturing fear, anger, dependence, and relief; end with “January, 1990.”
counterfactuals.output:
They say it will only be a moment.

Only—
that word with its clean hands,
its clipped wings,
its little white lie.

The tube is lifted away
and the room changes shape.

Air becomes a locked door.
My chest is a house
no one remembered to build stairs in.

They turn me,
soap my shoulder,
my useless arm,
the body I live inside
like a tenant
who cannot reach the window.

Water runs warm along my ribs.
Their voices float above me—
careful, almost cheerful—
as if kindness could be measured
in folded towels.

I want to curse them.
I want to say
hurry
hurry
hurry

but my mouth is busy being empty,
my throat a small dark country
with no roads out.

I hate them
for having lungs
they do not think about.

I need them
with a need so complete
it feels like humiliation.

My eyes do what they can:
flare, plead, accuse.
One attendant notices.

“Almost done,” she says,
and I could kill her
for that almost.

Then the machine returns,
its steady animal breath,
its metal mercy.

Air enters me
like a reprieve,
like forgiveness I did not ask for,
like the world
deciding not to let go.

I lie clean,
furious,
alive.

January, 1990.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a confessional first-person poem about being bathed by caregivers while on a ventilator, including miscommunication with attendants, the mantra “It’s almost over,” and the sensation of returning to the “land of breathing.”
counterfactuals.output:
While the ventilator counted for me,  
its bright lung lifting and lowering  
the curtain of my chest,  
they came with basins, cloths,  
blue gloves snapped at the wrist,  
voices softened as if I were already  
halfway out of the room.

I wanted to say, Not so cold.  
I wanted to say, My shoulder, wait—  
the tube pulled like a root in my throat,  
and all my words became weather  
inside plastic.

One attendant thought I was angry.  
Another thought I was asleep.  
I blinked for yes and they read it as no,  
shook my head for pain and they turned me  
toward the light.  
My body had become a country  
whose language no one on duty spoke.

They washed me anyway:  
neck, ribs, the hollow under the arm,  
the places where shame still lived  
though I could not defend them.  
Warm water cooled quickly on my skin.  
A cloth traveled my hip, my thigh,  
my useless hands resting open  
like I had given up asking.

“It’s almost over,” someone said,  
and I held to it  
as if it were a railing above a dark stair.  
It’s almost over.  
The turn, the lift, the sheet, the tube.  
It’s almost over.  
The nakedness, the helplessness,  
the small humiliations of being kept alive.

But it was not only the bath.  
It was the long machine-night,  
the ceiling tiles, the alarms,  
the way my breath had been borrowed  
and returned in measured portions.

I confess: I hated them  
for saving me so impersonally.  
I loved them  
for touching me as if I could still come back.

And then, one morning,  
air entered me without permission  
from the machine.  
Ragged, shallow, mine.  
I crossed over coughing,  
dragged by pain and light,  
back to the land of breathing—  
that green, ordinary country  
where the mouth opens,  
and the invisible world rushes in.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a stark narrative poem from the perspective of a former person reduced to “something that must be washed every day,” with dark humor, bodily vulnerability, and imagery of air rushing back into the lungs.
counterfactuals.output:
**Daily Care**

I used to have a name  
with corners on it.

It could be signed, shouted,  
spat across a kitchen,  
printed under a photograph  
where I stood upright  
and looked almost responsible.

Now I am  
something that must be washed every day.

There is a schedule for me.  
A cheerful chart.  
Boxes ticked in blue.  
A saint with latex hands  
comes in humming murder  
through her teeth.

She says,  
Let’s get you freshened up.

As if I were a salad.  
As if I had spent the night  
wilting attractively  
beside the ham.

The basin arrives,  
warm as a captured animal.  
Cloths. Soap. Towels folded  
with the precision  
of apology.

My body is introduced to me  
in sections.

Here is the shoulder.  
Here is the hip.  
Here is the pale country  
where no flag survived.

Here is the place  
I once guarded fiercely  
with buttons, belts,  
bad decisions.

Now the room knows everything.  
The window knows.  
The plastic chair knows.  
The drain in the floor  
has taken my confession  
and gurgled no comment.

I would laugh  
if it did not require breath.

Still, sometimes,  
when they turn me—  
when the ribs open their little gates,  
when the sheet loosens its white grip—  
air rushes back into my lungs

like late guests  
forcing the door,

like debt collectors,

like a flock of black birds  
startled from the chimney  
of a burned house.

For one second  
I am occupied again.

Something enters  
and throws its coat  
over the furniture.

My chest rises.  
The room is shocked.  
Even I am surprised  
by the old machinery  
clanking into praise.

Then the coughing starts.

Excellent, she says.  
That’s very good.

I have become  
a weather event  
people congratulate.

A productive spasm.  
A damp trumpet.  
A miracle  
with phlegm on its chin.

She wipes my mouth.  
She wipes my neck.  
She lifts my arm  
as if checking a broken wing  
for meat.

The body goes on  
being loyal  
long after the kingdom  
has been overthrown.

It sweats.  
It leaks.  
It insists on its damp citizenship.  
It sends messages  
from provinces  
I no longer visit.

Pain is the mailman.  
He knows the address.

Every morning  
the water darkens slightly  
with proof.

I watch it take me away  
in manageable amounts.

Nobody says death.  
They say comfort.  
They say hygiene.  
They say, Almost done.

They say,  
You’re doing beautifully,

to the thing  
that must be rolled,  
the thing that must be rinsed,  
the thing with the old face  
still inconveniently attached.

I want to tell them  
I was cruel once.  
I was kissed in a stairwell.  
I stole pears.  
I drove too fast.  
I broke a heart  
and kept the pieces  
for warmth.

I want to tell them  
there were nights  
the air came into me freely,  
without negotiation,  
and left the same way,  
unescorted.

But the cloth is over my eyes.

Warm water.  
Cheap soap.  
A hand at the jaw  
turning me gently  
toward the light.

There, she says.

All clean.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write an intimate, unsettling free verse piece about a person who can only spend fifty minutes away from their breathing machine, fantasizing about air and becoming enraged by small delays during care.
counterfactuals.output:
Fifty minutes.

That is the length of my leash,  
the mercy of the battery,  
the mercy of plastic teeth  
unclenched from the wet flower of my mouth.

The room changes when the machine stops.

Not silence—  
never silence—  
but a kind of listening  
that leans too close.

I count in my ribs.  
I count in the blue under my nails.  
I count the nurse’s hands  
as they fold the towel once,  
twice,  
as if linen has all day.

Air is always showing off.

It lies in the curtains,  
fat and careless.  
It strolls under the door.  
It pours itself into other people  
without asking,  
without tubes,  
without the soft animal panic  
of alarms.

I dream of it obscenely.

Air in handfuls.  
Air bitten from apples.  
Air drunk cold from a glass.  
Air filling me until I am round,  
until I am weather,  
until I do not have to be grateful  
to a humming box  
for every borrowed mouthful.

“Just a minute,” someone says.

A minute.

I could skin a minute alive.

I could tear it from the clock  
with my teeth.  
I could put my fist through the cheerful face  
of anyone who believes  
a minute is small.

The strap catches.  
The cap rolls beneath the bed.  
A glove snaps.  
Someone laughs in the hall.

And inside me  
a dark dog rises,  
hackles made of bone.

I love them, these hands that clean me,  
turn me, lift me gently  
from one indignity to another.

I love them until they pause.

Until they search the drawer.  
Until they smooth the sheet.  
Until they say, almost tenderly,  
“Hold on.”

As if I am not holding.

As if holding is not the whole country  
where I have lived for years.

Forty-three minutes.

My lungs become two fists  
closing around nothing.  
My blood knocks at the walls.  
My tongue grows ancient.  
The ceiling lowers itself  
like a face.

I think of fields.

Not real fields—  
I have no use for real things—  
but fields made entirely of breathing,  
grass-blades inhaling,  
soil exhaling,  
clouds swollen with the kind of air  
that enters without permission.

I walk there with no machine behind me.

No hose.  
No mask.  
No numbered mercy.  
Only my own chest  
opening and opening,  
an unlocked door  
in a house no one owns.

Then the caregiver fumbles.

One small delay.  
One stupid human second.

And I am all teeth.

I am rage in a hospital gown.  
I am the alarm before the alarm.  
I am begging and cursing  
with the same ruined breath.

Because fear is not delicate.

It does not wait its turn.  
It does not say please  
when the water rises.

Forty-nine minutes.

The machine is wheeled close,  
my faithful jailer,  
my obscene angel.

The mask returns.

The seal tightens.

Air enters me  
with its cold, mechanical devotion,  
and I hate it  
the way the drowned  
must hate the shore—

on their knees,  
alive,  
spitting salt,  
clutching the sand.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate a poem dated January 1990 about ventilator dependence, attendants washing an immobilized body, panic when words fail, and the ecstatic violence of being reconnected to breath.
counterfactuals.output:
**January 1990**

Morning enters as a basin of warm water,  
a towel folded over one shoulder,  
hands I did not raise  
turning me gently toward the light.

They wash the body I have become  
as if rinsing a stone found in a river—  
under the arms, behind the knees,  
the places where shame used to live  
before usefulness left me.

I try to say wait,  
or pain,  
or not like that,  
but the words strike glass inside my mouth.  
My tongue is a locked ward.  
My eyes flare,  
small trapped animals in the skull.

Then panic:  
the room widens,  
faces float away,  
the machine’s rhythm stumbles  
or I do—  
and all language is suddenly  
a country without roads.

I am only need.  
I am only the red alarm  
opening its metal throat.

Someone runs.  
Someone knows the ritual:  
tube, cuff, valve, the hard bright mercy  
of hands returning me  
to the engine of air.

And then breath comes back  
not softly, not like grace,  
but like being seized by the heavens  
and shaken alive—  
a brutal blue kiss,  
a fist of wind shoved into the chest,  
the ecstatic violence  
of the world insisting:

again.  
again.  
again.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
